chunks: Board techniques to protect against EMI. The question: What are some board-level techniques to protect against EMI?
To protect a circuit from outside interference, you build layers. At the connector, you add a surge-clamping diode and a filter so noise is stopped where it enters.
At each sensitive input, you add a small filter and keep wires short. In the layout, you keep loops small and bond connector shells to the enclosure. Shielding comes last.
Think of a castle. The moat and gatehouse are the connector protection, and they stop most trouble at the border. An inner wall is the small filter at each sensitive input.
The treasure sits in the middle, away from the gate. A tall outer wall, the shield, is costly, so it comes last.
The TVS sits at the connector with the shortest possible return; the bead blocks RF from entering the board; the RC at the receiving end finishes the job before the amplifier.
All the shunt parts return to the same low-impedance reference.
TVS diode: a protective diode that clamps a surge or static zap to a safe voltage.
Low-pass filter: a circuit, such as a resistor and capacitor, that passes slow signals and blocks fast noise. Corner frequency: the frequency where a filter starts to cut.
For an RC filter it is 1 over (2 pi RC) . Ferrite bead: a small part that acts like a resistor for fast noise, absorbing it.
Chassis bond: connecting a connector's metal shell to the enclosure with a short, wide path.
Put a 1 kilohms resistor and a 1 nanofarads capacitor in front of a sensor amplifier. The corner is about 159 kilohertz, so a slow sensor signal passes.
Noise at 100 megahertz is about 630 times above the corner, and an ideal filter cuts it by about that factor (56 decibels).
Real capacitors lose effect at high frequency, so use short leads.

At the connector, the TVS needs a short, wide return: a loop with 10 nanohenries of inductance (how strongly wiring fights fast current changes) and a static edge rising 10 amps per nanosecond adds 100 volts.
That is the whole idea: stop noise at the entry, then harden the victim.
"I defend in layers.
At every connector: a TVS for transients with a short, wide return to chassis, a ferrite bead or common-mode choke for RF, and a small capacitor, all placed right at the connector.
At the victim: an RC filter at sensitive inputs, low and balanced source impedance, short high-impedance traces.
In the layout: solid planes for small loops, differential signalling, partitioning away from connectors, and chassis bonding of shells.
Shielding and firmware robustness (watchdog, filtered resets) come after."
